summary: This RFC defines an extension to the Extensible Provisioning Protocol letting clients manage the Time-to-Live value for domain name delegation records. Registrars can then set how long resolvers may cache them through EPP.

eli5.summary: Every address-book entry says how long to trust it before checking again. This lets the people who register website names set that timer.

questions: how to set delegation ttl via epp
what is the epp ttl extension
what is policy mode in epp info
subtitle: How a domain registrar can set the DNS cache lifetime of delegation records through EPP.

tldr.problem: A registry normally decides the Time-to-Live of the delegation records it publishes, so a domain's sponsor cannot shorten it to speed up a change of DNS servers or a DNSSEC key rollover.
tldr.mechanism: An EPP extension adds a ttl element to the domain and host mappings. Clients set a TTL per record type in create and update commands, and read current values and server limits with an info command.
tldr.outcome: Registrars can manage delegation TTLs within the registry's policy. Servers may still override values for security or stability, and the RFC warns about fast flux DNS and compromised accounts.

facts.label: Record types
facts.value: NS, DS, DNAME, A, AAAA, custom

today: RFC 9803 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it is the definition of the EPP TTL extension.

sections.title: Why Delegation TTLs Need Managing
sections.content:
The main output of a domain name registry is a DNS zone file holding the delegation records for the names registered in a zone, such as a top-level domain. These usually include NS records, and may include DS records for DNSSEC-secured domains and DNAME records for IDN variants. A and AAAA records may also be published for nameservers where resolvers need them to avoid an infinite loop.

Typically the registry operator decides the Time-to-Live (TTL) of these records. In some cases the sponsoring client of a domain should be able to change it, for example to shorten the time needed to switch DNS servers, deploy DNSSEC or roll a key, or to allow a fast rollback of such changes.

RFC 9803 therefore extends the EPP domain mapping (RFC 5731) and host mapping (RFC 5732) so the sponsor of a domain or host object can change TTLs. It also says how servers should treat the values clients send.
sections.eli5: Normally the keeper of the big address book decides how long each entry may be remembered. Sometimes the owner needs a shorter timer so a change shows up quickly, so this lets the owner ask for one.

sections.title: The ttl Element and Its Attributes
sections.content:
The extension adds one main element, <ttl:ttl>, which gives the TTL of the DNS records for one record type. Its content is either a non-negative integer, the TTL in seconds, or empty, which means the server's default TTL for that type is applied.

The for attribute is required in commands and responses and names the record type: NS, DS, DNAME, A, AAAA or custom. With custom, a custom attribute carries a record type that matches the expression in RFC 6895 and is registered with IANA, so future record types need no new RFC.

The attributes min, default and max MUST NOT appear in commands but MAY appear in responses, where the server uses them to show the lowest, default and highest value a client may set. min MUST be lower than max, and default MUST lie between them inclusive.
sections.eli5: Each entry is a little label saying which kind of record it is and how many seconds it may be remembered. A blank label means use the usual timer.

sections.title: Reading TTLs with the Info Command
sections.content:
The EPP <info> command for domains and hosts gains an optional <ttl:info> extension element with a boolean policy attribute that defaults to false. It selects one of two modes.

  • Default mode (policy is 0 or false): the response MUST contain <ttl:ttl> elements for every record type that has a non-default TTL, without min, default or max.
  • Policy mode (policy is 1 or true): the response MUST contain elements for all supported record types, whether or not the object uses them, and each MUST carry min, default and max.

Policy mode is how a client discovers which record types the server lets it change and within what limits.
sections.eli5: A client can ask the keeper either "which timers have been changed from normal?" or "what are all the timers and the shortest and longest allowed?"

sections.title: Setting TTLs with Create and Update
sections.content:
The <create> and <update> commands for domains and hosts MAY carry an extension element, <ttl:create> or <ttl:update>, which MUST hold one or more <ttl:ttl> elements. An empty element asks for the server default.

If a value is outside the server's permitted range, the server MUST reject the command with a 2004 "Parameter value range error". Servers MUST restrict the accepted record types to those registered with IANA and appropriate above a zone cut. A command setting a TTL for an inapplicable or restricted type MUST get a 2306 "Parameter value policy" error. A and AAAA TTLs may be set on host objects but not on domain objects, unless the server uses the host attribute model.

A server MAY allow only some types, for example DS records only. Servers SHOULD publish the client's values in the DNS, but operators MAY disregard them for security and stability reasons.
sections.eli5: The owner can set a timer when first signing up or later. If the timer is too long, too short or for a record the keeper does not allow, the keeper says no with an error code.

sections.title: Out-of-Band Changes and Operations
sections.content:
Server operators MAY change TTL values out-of-band, meaning not in reply to a client <update>, to address operational or security issues. They MAY also reset TTLs to the default some time after an update, and MAY tell the sponsoring client using the EPP Change Poll Extension (RFC 8590).

Registries must balance registrants' wish to see changes quickly against the extra query traffic short TTLs bring. They SHOULD set minimum and maximum limits narrower than the XML schema allows, which accepts any value from 0 to 2147483647. If a registry changes its policy, existing client values may fall outside it, and the RFC places no obligation on operators about them.

A common mistake is to change a TTL during or after the planned change. A shorter TTL only helps if it is made at least one current TTL period before the change, plus the delay before the server publishes it. The RFC RECOMMENDS giving users this guidance.
sections.eli5: If you want people to forget an old address fast, you must shorten the timer well before you move, not on moving day.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Two risks are named. The first is fast flux DNS, where malicious actors rapidly change a zone's DNS configuration to evade takedown. A short delegation TTL may help that evasion, so server operators should weigh this when setting the lower limit, and client interfaces should consider controls that deter abuse.

The second is a compromised registrar account. An attacker could change NS or glue records and then raise the TTLs so the changes stay cached long after discovery. Client interfaces should therefore consider upper limits, alongside credential management, multi-factor authentication and risk-based access control.
sections.eli5: A timer that is too short helps bad guys hop around quickly. A timer that is too long locks in a bad change for ages, so both ends need sensible limits.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Formal Syntax
sections.content:
IANA registered the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:epp:ttl-1.0 and the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:epp:ttl-1.0, and listed the extension in the EPP extensions registry (RFC 7451) with status Active and TLDs set to Any.

Section 8 gives the full XML schema. It allows a TTL from 0 to 2147483647, requires the for attribute, and ensures each record type appears only once per command or response.
sections.eli5: The extension got its official name tag in the standard registry, and a rulebook describes exactly what a valid message looks like.

items.title: for
items.text: Required. Record type: NS, DS, DNAME, A, AAAA or custom.

items.title: custom
items.text: Record type name when for is custom; must be registered with IANA.

items.title: min
items.text: Responses only. Lowest value the client may set.

items.title: default
items.text: Responses only. The server's default value.

items.title: max
items.text: Responses only. Highest value the client may set.
